The [Prime Number Checker](/prime-number-checker) is a free online tool on CalcHub. Check whether an integer is prime and see its nearest primes. Check whether an integer is prime and see its nearest primes. This free online prime number checker gives you an instant answer without an account, a download or sending your entries to a server. It is designed for quick everyday use on desktop and mobile. This guide explains how to use it, the formula it applies, and a worked example you can follow with your own numbers.

## How to use the Prime Number Checker

Start by entering your positive integer. The result updates as you type, so adjust any value and watch the answer change. If the answer is not what you expected, check the value you entered first — a missing digit or a wrong unit is the usual cause. When you want a clean slate, Reset restores the defaults. The steps below walk through each input in order.

1. Enter your positive integer.
2. Check the result — it updates instantly as you type.
3. Use Reset to start over with the default values.

## Formula

A prime has exactly two positive divisors: 1 and itself. Test divisors only up to √n.

That is the standard formula for this calculation, and it is the same one the [Prime Number Checker](/prime-number-checker) applies to the values you enter. You can work it out by hand, but the calculator is faster when you want to try several values, and it removes the risk of a slip in the arithmetic. If the figures look wrong, check your inputs first — a misplaced decimal point is the usual culprit.

## Worked example

Here is a typical example. 97 is prime; 91 is not because 91 = 7 × 13. ## Tips

A few things worth knowing before you rely on the result — most of them are about the numbers you put in, rather than the tool itself:

- Check the units and labels before comparing results.
- Your entries stay in your browser and are not saved.

Keep these in mind and the figures will be as useful as the numbers you put in.

A prime has exactly two positive divisors: 1 and itself. Test divisors only up to √n. You can see it in action in the [Prime Number Checker](/prime-number-checker) — enter your own values and the result updates as you type.
